reading.translation:
Xenophon describes the education of the Spartans. The boys were educated by the supervisor of boys. He was a citizen and had authority.

The boys were taught to obey. They did not always have shoes; for they walked with bare feet. They wore one cloak throughout the year.

Little food was prepared for the boys. The account also includes theft of food. But the boy who was caught was punished, for he did not carry out the act secretly.

Xenophon praises endurance. We also ask about the boys. Who chose the education: the boys or those governing the city?

In a teaching example the boy appeared brave and answered the teacher. Not everyone who suffered was well educated. For suffering does not always provide good judgment.

What will result from the education? The young man will be educated and tested. But who will protect him? The safety of the boys and the virtue of the citizens are worthy of discussion.

blocks.title: παιδεύω and πείθομαι
body: παιδεύω means educate or train; πείθομαι can mean obey or be persuaded. These meanings are related in this scene but are not identical. Being trained does not itself establish that someone has freely agreed.
The passive ἐπαιδεύθη, “was educated,” names what happened to a person. Questions about purpose, authority, and consent require more than parsing that form.

sections.title: 1. First aorist passive
body: The first aorist passive uses a stem in -θη- with active-shaped secondary endings: ἐλύθην, ἐλύθης, ἐλύθη. These endings do not make the meaning active. The stem, principal parts, and context identify the passive.

The infinitive λυθῆναι and participle λυθείς, λυθεῖσα, λυθέν lack the indicative augment. Consonants may change before θ: διδάσκω has ἐδιδάχθην. Learn the passive principal part rather than attaching -θην blindly.

checks.answer: Its -θη- stem identifies the aorist passive.

sections.title: 2. Second aorist passive
body: A second aorist passive has -η- rather than -θη-: γράφω has ἐγράφην, “I was written/inscribed,” and φαίνω has ἐφάνην, often “I appeared.” The label describes formation; some passive-shaped forms have an intransitive meaning.
Compare ἐγράφην with ἐλύθην. Both use the same personal endings, but their passive stems differ. Infinitive γραφῆναι and participle γραφείς follow the same non-indicative pattern without augment.

sections.title: 3. Future passive
body: The future passive is built on the aorist passive stem with -σ- and middle endings: λυθήσομαι, “I shall be released.” A second-passive stem likewise gives γραφήσομαι. Unlike the aorist indicative, these futures have no augment.
Keep future active λύσω, future middle λύσομαι, and future passive λυθήσομαι distinct. The future passive infinitive is λυθήσεσθαι. An expressed personal agent can still use ὑπό plus genitive.

sections.title: 4. Deponents and responsible translation
body: Deponent verbs do not all form the aorist the same way. ἀποκρίνομαι has ἀπεκρινάμην, “I answered,” with middle aorist forms. βούλομαι has ἐβουλήθην, “I wished,” with passive-shaped aorist forms. Neither requires an English passive.

Record the principal part and the meaning together. Distinguish morphological description from translation: ἐβουλήθην is passive in formation but means “I wished.” The question “who chose the training?” must still be answered from the narrative.

sections.title: Meet the Constitution of the Lacedaemonians
body: Xenophon’s Constitution of the Lacedaemonians describes and evaluates Spartan institutions, often attributing their distinctive features to Lycurgus. “Constitution” here means an account of a community’s arrangements and way of life, not a modern written constitution with numbered rights.

This compact treatise asks how a relatively small community achieved exceptional power. Across fifteen chapters Xenophon discusses upbringing, common meals, habits concerning wealth, obedience, military organization, and kingship. He attributes the distinctive system to Lycurgus. The arrangement encourages readers to connect public strength with the repeated practices that form citizens from childhood onward.

The work is an argument about institutions, not simply a list of spectacular Spartan customs. Xenophon repeatedly contrasts Sparta with other Greek communities and admires the discipline he describes. Yet chapter 14 criticizes contemporary departures from the old standards. That tension lets us ask whether he is describing everyday reality, an ideal order, or the distance between the two.

Reading invitation: read chapter 2 on boys’ education alongside chapter 5 on common meals and chapter 14 on decline. Who supervises conduct, and what makes the system enforceable? Ask also whose lives receive less attention: women, noncitizens, and the enslaved helot population cannot be understood from the citizen-training account alone. In the linked combined volume, choose The Polity of the Lacedaemonians; the separate Athenian treatise is not generally accepted as Xenophon’s work.

Chapter 2 discusses boys’ education and contrasts Spartan practices with those of other Greeks. Xenophon often admires the system. His admiration is part of the evidence we must interpret; it does not make the account an impartial description of every child’s experience.

sections.title: A public supervisor, a disciplined body
body: The paidonomos, a public supervisor of boys, has authority in Xenophon’s account. Bare feet, limited clothing, and controlled food supply form part of a program intended to cultivate endurance and resourcefulness.

The passage also includes taking food secretly and punishment when caught. Describe that unsettling detail accurately before evaluating it. The lesson does not turn punishment or deprivation into a model for students to imitate.

sections.title: The missing viewpoint
body: A program can look successful from the viewpoint of the authority directing it while imposing costs on those undergoing it. The boys’ voices are not represented in the same way as Xenophon’s explanation of the institutions.

Ask what additional evidence you would want: experiences of participants, outcomes over time, or comparison with alternatives. State which question the passage can help answer and which it cannot answer by itself.

sections.title: Put the agent back in
body: Change “the boys were trained” into an active sentence naming the supervisor. Then ask who selected the goals and who had power to refuse. The passive is useful, but it can make authority less visible.

Design one imaginary training activity with a clear skill goal and a stopping rule. Explain how its usefulness would be judged. This is a modern discussion exercise, not a proposed reconstruction of an ancient Spartan regulation.
